passage:
Sahil, you look like the world has ended. Let me tell you what happened to me. I'm Farida, and at twenty-one, two days before my final project was due, my laptop died and the only copy went with it. I sat on the hostel stairs shaking. My roommate Uzma sat beside me and asked, "How much will this matter in a year?"
I said, "Everything." She said, "To whom?" I thought: my professor, my parents, me. In a year my professor would have marked forty other projects. My parents would care that I was well. I would care that I had finished something.
It still hurt. But the crash felt smaller, and I went to my professor that evening and asked for two extra days. She gave me one. I rewrote it in twenty hours and passed.

qa.q: How many extra days did Farida ask for, and how many did she get?
qa.a: Farida asked for two extra days and the professor gave one.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling on the hostel stairs?
qa.a: Farida was panicked and in deep distress, shaking and saying the crash mattered to everything. The fear was real, not just drama.

qa.q: What turning point in the story let Farida act instead of freezing?
qa.a: Uzma's questions about how much it would matter in a year, and to whom. Working through them made the problem smaller and let Farida go and ask the professor for time.

qa.q: Why might Uzma have asked questions and not simply said everything would be fine?
qa.a: Uzma could see that Farida's pain was real. The questions let Farida do the zooming out without being told how, which plain reassurance could not have done. 🤍

grounding: An elder recalls asking how much a disaster would matter in a year and to whom, which cut the drama without denying the pain.

passage:
Rain had ripped the tarp off the fest stall at 7:40 am, and the gates opened at 9. Shankar stood in a puddle, holding a sodden banner, his jaw tight. Every poster he had painted for two weeks was smeared. "It's ruined," he said. "Everything's ruined."
Kavitha, stapling a spare cloth to the frame beside him, didn't tell him to calm down. "Okay. In a year, who will remember this?" Shankar laughed shakily. "Me. Probably my parents, because I'll tell them." "And who would have noticed the posters?" "Maybe the first ten people who walk by."
He wiped his face. It still stung. But he picked up the marker and started on a fresh sign with a bigger, simpler design, and by 8:55 it was drying under the cloth.

qa.q: What time did the gates open?
What was Shankar feeling as he stood in the puddle holding the ruined banner?
qa.a: He was hurt and overwhelmed. His tight jaw and his declaring everything ruined show how much the two weeks of work meant to him.

qa.q: What small step got Shankar moving again?
qa.a: Answering Kavitha's questions about who would remember shrank the disaster, so he picked up a marker and started a simpler sign.

qa.q: How might Kavitha have felt while Shankar was upset and time was running out?
qa.a: Kavitha was probably worried and focused. Kavitha kept stapling the cloth rather than telling Shankar to calm down, which respects his feelings while helping with the deadline.

grounding: A young adult facing a fest-stall disaster asks how much it will matter in a year and to whom; the pain remains but shrinks.
